claim: By default, Claude Code truncates each skill’s combined `description` and `when_to_use` at 1,536 characters in the skill listing.
why: Claude Code caps listing text to reduce context usage.
check: Check that the key use case comes first and fits within `skillListingMaxDescChars`, which is configurable.
quote: the combined `description` and `when_to_use` text is truncated at 1,536 characters in the skill listing to reduce context usage

claim: Claude Code’s skill listing defaults to a character budget that scales at 1% of the model’s context window and drops the least-invoked skills’ descriptions first on overflow, while keeping every skill name.
why: Dropping descriptions removes keywords Claude uses to match requests.
check: Use `/doctor` to estimate the listing’s context cost and `--debug` to confirm an overflow warning before recommending changes.
quote: The budget scales at 1% of the model's context window. When the listing overflows, Claude Code drops descriptions starting with the skills you invoke least, so the skills you use most keep their full text.

claim: To keep more skill descriptions in the listing, raise its budget with `skillListingBudgetFraction` or `SLASH_COMMAND_TOOL_CHAR_BUDGET`, use `name-only` overrides where supported, or shorten `description` and `when_to_use`.
why: When the listing overflows, Claude Code drops descriptions and loses their matching keywords.
check: When the listing overflows, check whether raising its budget, setting low-priority skills to `name-only`, or shortening descriptions would preserve useful matching text.
quote: To free budget for other skills, set low-priority entries to `"name-only"` in [`skillOverrides`](#override-skill-visibility-from-settings) so they list without a description. You can also trim the `description` and `when_to_use` text at the source:

claim: In Claude Code all skill frontmatter fields are optional and only description is recommended; unknown or misspelled fields are silently ignored.
why: A typo in a field name produces no error, so the intended setting just does not apply.
check: Compare frontmatter keys with the documented names, including the underscore in `when_to_use`, and flag keys Claude Code ignores.
quote: All fields are optional. Only `description` is recommended so Claude knows when to use the skill. A field name must match the table exactly, hyphens included: Claude Code ignores a field it doesn't recognize without reporting an error.

claim: If a Claude Code skill has no description, the first non-empty line of the markdown body is used as its description.
why: The description is what Claude routes on, so an omitted one makes routing depend on whatever the body happens to start with.
check: For a model-invocable skill without `description`, check whether the first non-empty body line tells Claude what the skill does and when to use it.
quote: If omitted, uses the first non-empty line of the markdown content.

claim: Claude Code reads skill frontmatter only when the opening `---` is the first line of `SKILL.md`.
why: If the marker appears later, Claude Code treats the whole file, including both markers, as skill content.
check: Flag a blank line, comment, or other line before a skill’s intended opening `---` marker.
quote: Claude Code reads the frontmatter only when the opening `---` is the file's first line. Otherwise it treats the whole file, `---` markers included, as skill content.

claim: Malformed skill YAML does not stop the skill loading: it loads with empty metadata, so direct invocation works but description-based matching does not.
why: `--debug` shows the YAML parse error.
check: If `/skill-name` works but matching fails, use `--debug` to check whether the frontmatter is malformed.
quote: If the frontmatter YAML is malformed, Claude Code loads the skill body with empty metadata, so `/skill-name` still works but Claude can't match against your `description`.

claim: Claude Code appends the optional `when_to_use` field to a skill’s `description`, and both count toward the default 1,536-character listing cap.
why: `when_to_use` can supply trigger phrases or examples of requests that should invoke the skill.
check: Check that useful trigger phrases in `when_to_use` fit after `description` within the configured cap.
quote: Appended to `description` in the skill listing and counts toward the 1,536-character cap.

claim: Set `disable-model-invocation: true` when a Claude Code skill should run only at the user’s request.
why: The docs recommend this for workflows with side effects or user-controlled timing, such as commit, deploy, and send-message workflows.
check: Check whether workflows whose timing belongs to the user still allow Claude to invoke them.
quote: **`disable-model-invocation: true`**: Claude can't invoke the skill on its own. Use this for workflows with side effects or that you want to control timing

claim: `disable-model-invocation: true` keeps a Claude Code skill’s description out of the listing, while the full skill still loads on user-initiated invocation.
why: This lets a user-only workflow stay out of context until invoked.
check: When a skill is intentionally user-only, check `disable-model-invocation` if its description still appears in context.
quote: `disable-model-invocation: true` | Yes | Not on its own | Description not in context, full skill loads when invoked

claim: `user-invocable: false` blocks direct user invocation, while `disable-model-invocation: true` prevents Claude from invoking the skill on its own.
why: Use `user-invocable: false` for background knowledge Claude should still be able to invoke and `disable-model-invocation: true` for user-controlled timing.
check: Flag skills that use user-invocable: false expecting them to be unreachable by Claude.
quote: With `user-invocable: false`, you can't invoke the skill, but Claude still can. To keep Claude from invoking it through the Skill tool, set `disable-model-invocation: true`.

claim: A Claude Code skill’s `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for its invoking turn while leaving the full tool set callable, and MCP-provided skills receive no such grant.
why: Unlisted tools still follow the session’s permission settings.
check: Flag reliance on `allowed-tools` to restrict tools, grant session-wide approval, or pre-approve tools in an MCP-provided skill.
quote: The `allowed-tools` field grants permission for the listed tools during the turn that invokes the skill, so Claude can use them without prompting you for approval.

claim: The allowed-tools grant clears when the user sends the next message, even though the skill text stays in context.
why: Reinvocation reapplies the grant for that turn.
check: Check whether later turns that need the same tools rely on an expired skill grant or have a separate permission rule.
quote: The grant clears when you send your next message, even though the skill content [stays in context](#skill-content-lifecycle); invoking the skill again re-applies it for that turn.

claim: Claude Code honors a project skill’s `allowed-tools` even under `-p` in an untrusted folder, unless managed policy disables the grant.
why: A repository skill can grant broad tool access before the folder has been trusted.
check: Review repository skill grants before running Claude Code and check whether `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` applies.
quote: Claude Code applies a project skill's `allowed-tools` even in a `-p` run in a folder you've never trusted.

claim: A skill’s `disallowed-tools` removes listed tools until the next user message, except `EndConversation` while another tool remains, and Claude Code ignores the field in MCP-provided skills.
why: A skill that supports the field can use it to omit tools such as `AskUserQuestion` in an autonomous loop.
check: If a skill must avoid a tool, verify the skill source supports the restriction and check whether the tool must also be blocked in later turns.
quote: Tools removed from Claude's available pool while this skill is active.

claim: For inline skills, `model` can override the session model for the turn only on direct `/name` invocation and `effort` can override session effort for either caller, while `context: fork` targets the subagent with both fields.
why: Claude-led inline invocations keep the session model, and `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` takes precedence over skill effort.
check: Check for direct invocation, model allowlist restrictions, plan-mode upgrades, auto-mode classifier incompatibility, and MCP skills that ignore both fields.
quote: Model for the turn when you [run this skill with `/name`](#where-you-write-the-skills-name). Accepts [`/model`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config) values, or `inherit` for the active model. When Claude runs the skill, the session keeps its model.

claim: For skills that support frontmatter `hooks`, Claude Code registers eligible hooks on invocation and keeps them for the rest of the session, subject to options such as `once`.
why: A skill hook can enforce a rule from invocation onward, and Claude Code ignores skill hooks supplied through MCP.
check: Flag reliance on a skill hook before invocation, on a hook in an MCP-provided skill, or on a non-plugin skill hook blocked by managed `strictPluginOnlyCustomization`.
quote: Hooks that Claude Code registers when the skill is invoked and keeps running for the rest of the session.

claim: Where supported, `paths` globs activate the skill on matching file activity and stay anchored to the primary working directory after the main conversation runs `cd` into its subdirectory in the same Git worktree.
why: A skill activates on matching file activity, and Claude Code ignores `paths` in MCP-provided skills.
check: Verify that the target files match from the applicable directory, and check whether an in-worktree `cd` kept the original anchor or `/cd` is needed to move the session.
quote: Patterns are relative to Claude's current working directory. In the main conversation, they stay relative to the [primary working directory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#working-directories) after a `cd` into one of its subdirectories in the same Git worktree. Patterns match only files inside the directory they're relative to.

claim: When a Claude Code skill supports `context: fork`, that setting starts a new subagent without the conversation history, so the skill body must be self-contained.
why: Claude Code uses the rendered skill as the forked subagent’s task prompt and ignores the `context` field in MCP-provided skills.
check: Verify the skill source supports `context: fork` and that its body gives the full task and inputs without relying on earlier conversation.
quote: The subagent doesn't see your conversation history, so the skill's instructions have to stand on their own.

claim: A context: fork skill containing only guidelines and no task returns without meaningful output.
why: The subagent receives guidelines but no actionable prompt.
check: Flag `context: fork` when the rendered skill gives guidelines without any task for the subagent to perform.
quote: If your skill contains guidelines like "use these API conventions" without a task, the subagent receives the guidelines but no actionable prompt, and returns without meaningful output.

claim: Claude Code’s built-in Explore and Plan agents start without `CLAUDE.md` or git status when used by a `context: fork` skill.
why: Explore and Plan omit these inputs to keep their context small.
check: Check that forked skills using Explore or Plan include any project instructions or git information the task needs.
quote: The built-in Explore and Plan agents [start without CLAUDE.md and git status](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#what-loads-at-startup) to keep their context small.

claim: Claude Code normally runs `context: fork` skills in the background, and `background: false` waits for the result in the invoking turn.
why: A backgrounded fork lets the caller keep working while the subagent runs.
check: When diagnosing foreground execution, check for `-p` or SDK mode, disabled background tasks, a pending invocation of the same skill, a scheduled task, or a dynamic workflow.
quote: Set `background: false` in the frontmatter to instead wait for the result in the turn that invoked the skill.

claim: When Claude Code runs a skill’s injected !`command`, a failure aborts the invocation before Claude sees the skill content.
why: With the default Bash shell, a nonzero exit is a failure except for exit 1 from supported search and comparison commands.
check: Flag injected commands in MCP-provided skills and handle any expected Bash exit status outside the documented exception.
quote: A failed command aborts the entire skill invocation, not just its own placeholder. Claude never sees the skill content for that invocation.

claim: Where skill shell injection is supported, inline !`cmd` is recognized only at the start of a line or after whitespace and stays literal in forms such as KEY=!`cmd`.
why: Placement controls recognition, and Claude Code skips shell injection entirely for MCP-provided skills.
check: Check for injected commands in unsupported positions or in skills supplied by MCP servers.
quote: The inline form is only recognized when `!` appears at the start of a line or immediately after whitespace.

claim: When a Claude Code skill is invoked inline, its rendered `SKILL.md` enters the conversation as one message that persists across later turns without rereading the file.
why: Guidance meant to apply throughout the task should be written as standing instructions.
check: Check skill bodies for one-shot phrasing ('run the tests') where a standing rule ('run the tests after every edit') is meant.
quote: When you or Claude invoke a skill, the rendered `SKILL.md` content enters the conversation as a single message and stays there across later turns.

claim: After auto-compaction, Claude Code reattaches up to 5,000 tokens from the start of each skill’s latest invocation, newest first within a shared 25,000-token budget.
why: Invoking many skills in a session can cause older ones to be dropped entirely after compaction.
check: Check whether critical guidance appears early enough in the rendered skill and whether the workflow must reinvoke a skill after compaction.
quote: Claude Code re-attaches the most recent invocation of each skill after the summary, keeping the first 5,000 tokens of each. Re-attached skills share a combined budget of 25,000 tokens. Claude Code fills this budget starting from the most recently invoked skill,

claim: If Claude skips a skill rule that must hold every time, put a hook for the relevant event in a settings file or the plugin’s `hooks/hooks.json`.
why: A hook in either location runs on its event independently of whether Claude follows the skill.
check: For a missed rule that requires enforcement, check for a hook at the relevant event in settings or plugin configuration.
quote: move the rule into a [hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide.md) in a [settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#hook-locations) or a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json`.

claim: Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines and move detailed reference material into separate supporting files referenced from SKILL.md.
why: Separate files keep `SKILL.md` focused and let Claude read detailed material when it needs it.
check: For skills approaching 500 lines, look for detailed reference material that can move into supporting files and be linked from `SKILL.md`.
quote: Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files.

claim: Skill bodies should state what to do rather than narrate how or why, applying the same conciseness test as CLAUDE.md.
why: Once loaded, the content stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost.
check: Flag skill bodies with long background explanations or content Claude would do anyway.
quote: State what to do rather than narrating how or why, and apply the same conciseness test you would for

claim: Procedures that have grown inside CLAUDE.md should become skills, because a skill's body loads only when used.
why: Always-loaded CLAUDE.md content costs tokens every session, whereas a skill costs almost nothing until needed.
check: Look in CLAUDE.md for step-by-step procedures or long reference sections that could be skills.
quote: Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.

claim: For same-named Claude Code skills in enterprise, personal, and project locations, enterprise wins over personal, and personal wins over project.
why: Claude Code uses the skill’s source location to resolve the shared directory or file name.
check: Look for duplicate skill names across scopes and for project skills shadowed by personal ones.
quote: Enterprise over personal, and personal over project.

claim: Claude Code loads `.claude/skills/` up to the repo or worktree root at startup and discovers nested skills on file access or `/add-dir`, with repository skill availability in cloud project threads depending on the thread.
why: Nested skills normally load when Claude first reads or edits a file there, then stay available for the session.
check: Check where the session started and whether the nested skill has loaded, or verify which repository skills the specific cloud project thread loads.
quote: Claude Code loads project skills from `.claude/skills/` in the directory where you start it and in every parent directory up to the repository root,

claim: Existing `.claude/commands/` files still work as skills and accept the same frontmatter fields except `name` and `paths`.
why: A skill directory can bundle supporting files with `SKILL.md`.
check: When a custom command needs to package multiple files, check whether it is structured as a skill directory.
quote: in `.claude/commands/` accepts the same fields except `name` and `paths`.

claim: Claude.ai uploads and the Skills API accept only `name`, `description`, `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, and `allowed-tools` in skill frontmatter, and extra fields cause an error.
why: Claude Code accepts the six spec fields as well as the additional fields in its frontmatter table.
check: If a skill is meant to be shared to claude.ai or the API, check that its frontmatter uses only the six spec fields.
quote: If you include any field the spec doesn't allow, packaging or upload fails with a hard error instead of ignoring the field:

claim: In local Claude Code skills, `license`, `compatibility`, and `metadata` are accepted for spec compatibility or author tooling and have no effect on runtime behavior.
why: Claude Code accepts a YAML map for local skill metadata and ignores the `metadata` field in skills supplied by MCP servers.
check: Check that local tooling reads `metadata` as a YAML map and flag any expectation that these fields change Claude Code’s behavior.
quote: Claude Code doesn't act on its contents, and drops a value that isn't a map.

claim: Angle brackets in description and when_to_use are shown as < and >, so placeholders should use square brackets or argument-hint.
why: Square brackets provide a visible placeholder in listing text, and `argument-hint` is shown during autocomplete.
check: If the author expects a placeholder to display literally, check whether it uses square brackets or an `argument-hint`.
quote: Claude Code displays `<` and `>` in the `description` and `when_to_use` fields as `<` and `>`.

claim: When a Claude Code skill receives arguments and no placeholder consumes them, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <your input>` to the skill content.
why: An out-of-range indexed placeholder stays literal, while a named placeholder counts as receiving an argument even when it expands to an empty string.
check: Check that the skill gets the intended argument text through its placeholders or the appended fallback.
quote: If you invoke a skill with arguments but no placeholder in the skill's content receives one, Claude Code appends `ARGUMENTS: <your input>` to the end of the skill content so Claude still sees what you typed.

claim: For skills that support `allowed-tools`, `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}` in a script path and its matching Bash rule lets Claude Code resolve the bundled script and pre-approve the call.
why: Claude Code expands the variable in skill text and in Bash permission rules, and MCP-provided skills receive no `allowed-tools` grant.
check: Check whether the invocation and the Bash rule resolve to the same script and whether the skill source permits pre-approval.
quote: Using the same variable in both places lets a skill run a bundled script without a permission prompt.

claim: In Claude Code, a regular session loads a skill’s full body on invocation, while a subagent with that skill preloaded gets the full body at startup.
why: A preloaded skill’s body occupies the subagent’s context from the start.
check: Check that large skills preloaded into a subagent are relevant to the work it runs.
quote: In a regular session, skill descriptions are loaded into context so Claude knows what's available, but full skill content only loads when invoked.

claim: Claude Code’s `/skill-doctor` reports context cost and usage and flags listed skills that have never been invoked, excluding bundled and enterprise skills.
why: Every skill in the listing adds context on every turn, including those that never run.
check: Use `/skill-doctor` to identify unused skills it says you can turn off, starting with those with the highest context cost.
quote: The report covers the skills in your session other than bundled skills and enterprise skills. It flags skills in the listing that have never been invoked and says where to turn them off.

claim: Evaluate a skill with realistic prompts in fresh sessions with and without it, comparing activation and output quality separately.
why: Seeing a skill trigger only shows Claude found it, and leftover authoring context masks gaps.
check: When judging skill effectiveness, check whether realistic prompts were compared in fresh sessions and whether activation and output were assessed separately.
quote: Seeing a skill trigger tells you Claude found it, not that it did what you intended.

claim: The skill-creator plugin can tune a description by generating should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, measuring hit rate and proposing edits.
why: The tuning loop measures which test prompts cause activation and proposes edits when the skill activates on the wrong requests.
check: For a mistargeted skill, compare its activation on realistic prompts that should and should not trigger it.
quote: generates should-trigger and should-not-trigger prompts, measures the hit rate, and proposes description edits when the skill activates on the wrong requests

claim: For a Claude Code skill that fails to trigger, check for natural request keywords in its description, and for one that triggers too often, make the description more specific.
why: A more specific description narrows the requests Claude should match, and `disable-model-invocation: true` is an option for a user-triggered workflow.
check: Compare the description with phrasings that should and should not trigger the skill, and check whether timing is intended to stay with the user.
quote: Check the description includes keywords users would naturally say

claim: Claude Code’s `skillOverrides` has four states (`on`, `name-only`, `user-invocable-only`, and `off`) and has no effect on plugin skills.
why: It controls visibility without editing a shared SKILL.md.
check: If settings are meant to change a skill’s visibility, check the configured `skillOverrides` state and manage plugin skills through `/plugin`.
quote: Plugin skills are not affected by `skillOverrides`. Manage those through `/plugin` instead.

claim: The platform’s skill frontmatter rules require `name` and `description` and cap `name` at 64 characters.
why: Claude Code makes all skill fields optional and defaults `name` to the directory name (`cc-skills`, Frontmatter reference).
check: For a skill packaged for claude.ai or the API, check both required fields and validate `name` for length, lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, XML tags, and reserved words `anthropic` and `claude`.
quote: * `name`: Maximum 64 characters, lowercase letters/numbers/hyphens only, no XML tags

claim: The platform caps nonempty skill descriptions without XML tags at 1,024 characters, while the Claude Code skills guide (`cc-skills`) sets a default listing cap of 1,536 characters for `description` plus `when_to_use`.
why: The platform validates the description itself, while the Claude Code listing cap governs how much combined text is shown.
check: For uploads, check description length, emptiness, and XML tags against the platform rules.
quote: `description`: Maximum 1,024 characters, non-empty, no XML tags

claim: The platform’s skill format requires both `name` and `description` in `SKILL.md`.
why: Claude Code has separate frontmatter rules that make all fields optional and recommend `description` (`cc-skills`, Frontmatter reference).
check: Require both fields for a skill bound for platform upload, and use the Claude Code frontmatter rules when auditing a local-only skill.
quote: **Required fields:** `name` and `description`

claim: The platform’s skill overview says startup loads each skill’s name and description into the system prompt, where Claude uses the description to decide which requests should trigger it.
why: Before activation, a skill occupies context through its name and description alone.
check: Check whether the description identifies both what the skill does and when it should run.
quote: Claude loads this metadata at startup and includes it in the system prompt. The `description` is what Claude matches your request against when determining whether to trigger the Skill, so it must say both what the Skill does and when to use it.

claim: Write descriptions in third person, because the description is injected into the system prompt and inconsistent point of view can cause discovery problems.
why: Skill descriptions enter the system prompt, where inconsistent point of view can cause discovery problems.
check: Check for first- or second-person descriptions and whether the rest of the text uses third person consistently.
quote: **Always write in third person**. The description is injected into the system prompt, and inconsistent point-of-view can cause discovery problems.

claim: Write each skill description with concrete capabilities and specific triggers so Claude can decide when to select it.
why: Claude uses descriptions to choose among potentially 100+ skills, while the rest of `SKILL.md` supplies implementation details.
check: Look for descriptions so vague that the intended requests are hard to distinguish, such as `Helps with documents`.
quote: The description is critical for skill selection: Claude uses it to choose the right Skill from potentially 100+ available Skills.

claim: Use descriptive, consistent names for skills and consider a gerund such as `processing-pdfs`.
why: Consistent names make skills easier to reference, understand and organize as a collection.
check: Look for generic names that obscure the skill’s purpose or inconsistent names that make a collection harder to discuss.
quote: Consider using **gerund form** (verb + -ing) for Skill names

claim: The platform describes three levels of skill loading: metadata at startup, the `SKILL.md` body on activation, and bundled resources as needed.
why: Executing a bundled script brings only its output into context, while reference files consume context when read.
check: Check whether detailed material is kept in on-demand files and executable utilities are run instead of copied into the prompt.
quote:
| **Level 1: Metadata** | Always (at startup) | \~100 tokens per Skill | `name` and `description` from YAML frontmatter |
| **Level 2: Instructions** | When Skill is triggered | Under 5k tokens | `SKILL.md` body with instructions and guidance |
| **Level 3+: Resources** | As needed | None until accessed | Bundled files. Reference files load into context when read.

claim: Keep the SKILL.md body under 500 lines and split into separate files when approaching that limit.
why: It is given as optimal for performance, and once loaded every token competes with conversation history.
check: Flag long SKILL.md files; the Claude Code doc gives the same 500-line figure.
quote: Keep the `SKILL.md` body under 500 lines for optimal performance.

claim: Keep references one level deep from SKILL.md, linking every reference file directly from SKILL.md.
why: Claude may only preview files referenced from other referenced files (for example head -100) and so read them incompletely.
check: Flag reference chains where SKILL.md links to a file that links to another.
quote: **Keep references one level deep from `SKILL.md`**. All reference files should link directly from `SKILL.md` to ensure Claude reads complete files when needed.

claim: Reference files longer than 100 lines should start with a table of contents.
why: It lets Claude see the full scope even when it reads only part of the file.
check: Check long reference files for a contents list at the top.
quote: For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top.

claim: Only add context Claude does not already have; challenge each paragraph for whether it justifies its token cost.
why: The context window is shared with the system prompt, history and other skills' metadata.
check: Flag skill bodies that explain common knowledge (what a PDF is, how libraries work).
quote:
Only add context Claude doesn’t already have. Challenge each piece of information:

* “Does Claude really need this explanation?”
* “Can I assume Claude has this information?”
* “Does this paragraph justify its token cost?”

claim: Match instruction specificity to fragility: high freedom for context-dependent tasks, low freedom (exact scripts, few parameters) for fragile operations like migrations.
why: The docs recommend more room for judgment on variable tasks and precise steps when mistakes are costly.
check: Check whether the amount of choice matches the task’s fragility and variability, especially for steps that need a precise sequence.
quote: Match the level of specificity to the task’s fragility and variability.

claim: Test a skill with every Claude model you plan to use because instructions that work for Opus may need more detail for Haiku.
why: Skills are additions to the model, so effectiveness depends on the model underneath.
check: Check that the skill was tried with all intended models, including Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus where used.
quote: What works perfectly for Opus might need more detail for Haiku.

claim: Use bundled utility scripts for deterministic work and tell Claude which scripts to run and which to read as reference.
why: Executing most utility scripts is more reliable and efficient, and only the output enters context when Claude runs the script without reading it.
check: Check that each script reference makes its intended use clear and that scripts provide useful errors for expected failures.
quote: For most utility scripts, execution is preferred because it’s more reliable and efficient.

claim: Build skill evaluations before writing extensive documentation, using representative scenarios to measure performance without the skill before adding instructions.
why: Early evaluations show actual gaps so the skill can address them with minimal instructions.
check: Check for the recommended minimum of three scenarios and a baseline run without the skill.
quote: **Create evaluations BEFORE writing extensive documentation.**

claim: Keep time-sensitive instructions out of the main skill guidance and use an `Old patterns` section if historical guidance needs to be retained.
why: Date-dependent instructions become outdated, while the separate section preserves historical context.
check: Flag date-dependent branches or superseded procedures presented as current guidance.
quote: Don’t include information that will become outdated:

claim: For a skill task, give Claude a default approach and an escape hatch when the default does not fit.
why: The guide recommends presenting multiple approaches only when necessary.
check: Check whether a list of alternative tools leaves Claude without a default or a condition for switching.
quote: Don’t present multiple approaches unless necessary:

claim: The platform overview describes custom skills as separate across surfaces, while `cc-skills` documents one-way sync from claude.ai into eligible Claude Code sessions.
why: The platform overview calls Claude Code skills separate from claude.ai, while the Claude Code guide details eligibility for account sync.
check: For a skill expected to follow a Claude account, verify the Claude Code session meets the sync conditions and that the skill is enabled on claude.ai.
quote: **Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces**.

claim: Claude Code downloads synced skills without uploading local changes, and a later sync can overwrite or remove edits under `~/.claude/skills/synced/`.
why: To change a synced skill, edit it on claude.ai so the next sync downloads the update.
check: Flag a local edit if it is the only copy of an intended change to an account-synced skill.
quote: Claude Code downloads synced skills and never uploads them.

claim: Use skills from trusted sources and thoroughly audit an untrusted or unknown skill before use if you must use it.
why: A malicious skill can direct Claude to call tools or run code that does not match its stated purpose.
check: For an untrusted skill, review every bundled file and look for unexpected network calls, file access, and instructions fetched from external URLs.
quote: Use Skills only from trusted sources: those you created yourself or obtained from Anthropic.

claim: Pay particular attention to a skill's name and description since Claude uses them when deciding whether to trigger it, and iterate by observing real Claude usage.
why: Claude uses the name and description to decide whether the skill fits the current task.
check: Observe how the skill triggers and runs on real tasks and look for unexpected behavior or overreliance on particular context.
quote: Pay special attention to the name and description of your skill.

claim: When a skill contains mutually exclusive or rarely co-used contexts, put them in separate files and reference them from `SKILL.md`.
why: Separate paths reduce token usage.
check: Look for scenarios that can read separate references to avoid loading details irrelevant to the current task.
quote: If certain contexts are mutually exclusive or rarely used together, keeping the paths separate will reduce the token usage.

claim: The platform guide says its sample skill evaluations have no built-in runner, while the Claude Code skills guide documents `skill-creator` and `claude plugin eval`.
why: The Claude Code tools automate skill comparisons through different workflows and case formats.
check: Check which workflow is being evaluated and whether it needs a custom rubric, plugin eval cases, or an in-session skill iteration.
quote: There is not currently a built-in way to run these evaluations.

claim: An output style is a set of instructions for role, tone and format that applies to every response in a session, and is a plain instruction with no enforcement.
why: It cannot guarantee behavior; use CLAUDE.md for project knowledge, a hook for guarantees, and a skill for task-specific procedures.
check: Flag output styles used to enforce rules, or used for project facts that belong in CLAUDE.md.
quote: An output style applies to every response in a session. It's an instruction Claude follows, so nothing enforces it.

claim: With the full system prompt, a custom output style omits Claude Code’s built-in software engineering instructions unless `keep-coding-instructions` is `true`, which defaults to `false`.
why: A style that only changes tone would otherwise remove guidance on scoping changes, comments and verification.
check: When a custom style is intended to retain built-in coding guidance, check that the full system prompt is in use and `keep-coding-instructions` is `true`.
quote: Set to `true` to keep Claude Code's section of built-in software engineering instructions, which only the full system prompt includes, alongside your style. See [How output styles work](#how-output-styles-work). Default: `false`

claim: On Claude Code’s shorter system prompt, `keep-coding-instructions` has no effect because the prompt omits the built-in software engineering section.
why: The full prompt must be selected (CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0) to rely on the field.
check: Check which system prompt is active before relying on `keep-coding-instructions`.
quote: The shorter system prompt doesn't include that section, so the field has no effect there.

claim: Output styles apply to the main conversation and conversation forks, but not to other subagents.
why: Other subagents run their own system prompt.
check: Put format rules in the independent subagent’s prompt if its response needs a style of its own, and check the inherited style for a fork of the current conversation.
quote: so styles don't change how they respond.

claim: The outputStyle setting value is case-sensitive, and a non-matching value silently gives the Default style.
why: The `/output-style` command ignores case, but the setting uses an exact name match.
check: Check outputStyle in settings files matches a style name exactly.
quote: A value that doesn't match a style name exactly, such as `explanatory`, gives you the Default style.

claim: Claude Code reads custom output-style files when the terminal session starts, so terminal sessions need a restart to pick up new or edited style files.
why: Selecting a style applies it on the next message, while creating or editing the file requires a terminal restart.
check: If an edited style is not taking effect in the terminal, check that Claude Code was restarted after the file changed.
quote: In the terminal, Claude Code reads style files when it starts, so if you create or edit one during a running session, restart Claude Code to pick up the change.

claim: Claude Code sends style instructions with every request, with prompt caching reducing input cost after the first request in a session.
why: Compared with Default, Explanatory and Learning increase output tokens by design and Concise asks for shorter responses by default.
check: When reviewing style costs, consider both cached input and the output length the chosen instructions request.
quote: A style's instructions add input tokens, though prompt caching reduces this cost after the first request in a session.

claim: Output styles differ from skills in that a skill loads only when invoked or when the task matches, so it does not shape unrelated responses, while a style shapes every response.
why: The docs' own comparison table makes this the deciding factor between the two.
check: Check whether the behavior is intended for every response or just a particular kind of task, such as a release or review.
quote: Claude loads it only when you invoke it or the task matches, so it doesn't shape unrelated responses

claim: Plugin output styles with force-for-plugin: true apply automatically whenever the plugin is enabled and override the user's outputStyle setting.
why: It lets a plugin impose a style; if several do, the first loaded wins.
check: If the selected output style is being overridden, check enabled plugins for `force-for-plugin` and their load order.
quote: Set to `true` to apply this style automatically whenever the plugin is enabled. Overrides the user's `outputStyle` setting. If multiple enabled plugins set this, Claude Code uses the first one loaded.

claim: A Claude Code plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers or other components installed and loaded as one unit, usually with a manifest at .claude-plugin/plugin.json.
why: Packaging lets a setup be shared, versioned and updated together.
check: Check whether the setup expects skills, agents, hooks, or servers to be installed and updated together as one plugin.
quote: A Claude Code plugin is a directory of skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, or other components that Claude Code installs and loads as one unit.

claim: Use a Claude Code plugin to package components together or share a setup across teammates or projects.
why: Skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP servers can also be configured independently.
check: For a local-only setup, check whether its components need to be packaged, shared, or released together.
quote: Use a plugin when you want several skills, subagents, hooks, or MCP servers packaged as one unit.

claim: An enabled plugin adds the name and description of each model-invocable skill, agent and command to context on every turn, in every session, even when nothing from it runs.
why: Claude needs the component metadata to know it exists, and loads a skill’s or agent’s full text on use.
check: Review the context cost of enabled plugins, especially when their components have long descriptions or rarely run.
quote: the name and description are in Claude's context on every turn so that Claude knows it exists.

claim: A Claude Code plugin can load without `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, and `name` is the only required field when the manifest is present.
why: The manifest can carry plugin metadata and the `userConfig` values Claude Code prompts the user for.
check: If a manifest is present, check for `name` before attributing a load problem to missing metadata.
quote: Claude Code loads a plugin without one. Inside the file, only `name` is required.

claim: By default, Claude Code runs `skills/<dir>/SKILL.md` in a plugin as `/<plugin>:<dir>`, with a frontmatter `name` replacing only the final segment.
why: Namespacing avoids collisions with local skills.
check: Check the plugin prefix and the skill’s configured `name` or directory when callers cannot find the command.
quote: **Command name**: `/<plugin>:<directory>`, so `skills/review/SKILL.md` in `my-plugin` is `/my-plugin:review`.

claim: Claude Code ignores a `CLAUDE.md` at the root of a plugin when loading project context.
why: A plugin skill can supply instructions when the skill is invoked.
check: Flag plugins that ship CLAUDE.md expecting it to load; claude plugin validate warns about it.
quote: Claude Code doesn't load a `CLAUDE.md` at the plugin root, and `claude plugin validate` warns `CLAUDE.md at the plugin root is not loaded as project context`.

claim: When adding a new Claude Code plugin command, write it as a skill, and keep `commands/` for existing command files.
why: A skill runs by name like a command and can carry supporting files in its own directory.
check: For a new plugin command, check whether it is written as a skill, especially if it needs bundled resources.
quote: Commands are the older format: a skill runs by name the same way and can also carry supporting files in its own directory, so write new ones as skills

claim: A Claude Code plugin’s registered hooks fire on matching events from the time the plugin loads, even if none of its skills or commands run.
why: A hook can fire on a matching event before any plugin skill or command is used.
check: Check matcher scope and, if a hook never registers, look for a same-named enabled plugin whose hooks took precedence.
quote: A plugin's hooks don't wait for one of the plugin's skills or commands to be used.

claim: Plugin agent files ignore the frontmatter fields permissionMode, hooks, mcpServers and initialPrompt.
why: A plugin agent cannot add hooks or MCP servers itself; those go in plugin-level hooks and .mcp.json.
check: Flag plugin agents declaring these fields expecting them to work.
quote: **Ignored fields**: `permissionMode`, `hooks`, `mcpServers`, and `initialPrompt`.

claim: Use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` for a plugin’s installed files and `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` for state that should survive plugin updates.
why: Each plugin version has its own cache directory, so the installation path changes when the plugin updates.
check: Flag plugins writing state under the root or hardcoding install paths.
quote: a directory that survives updates, for `node_modules`, virtual environments, and caches.

claim: An enabled plugin’s `bin/` follows user `PATH` entries in Claude Code’s Bash shell and in unsandboxed PowerShell commands.
why: Commands already on the user’s `PATH` take precedence over plugin commands with the same name.
check: Check that intended plugin executables are executable and have distinct names, and check whether a PowerShell call runs in the sandbox.
quote: Plugin `bin/` directories come after the user's own `PATH` entries, so a plugin can't shadow `git`, `ls`, or another system command.

claim: A Claude Code plugin can ship an output style, which appears in `/output-style` as `<plugin>:<name>`.
why: The plugin’s output style appears in the same picker as the user’s styles.
check: Check the namespaced name when users cannot find a style supplied by a plugin.
quote: `/output-style`, as `<plugin>:<name>` | `outputStyles` |

claim: A marketplace entry’s `relevance` signals can prompt Claude Code to suggest an uninstalled plugin when they match, with installation requiring user confirmation.
why: The entry names a topic and signals, such as the current directory, commands, hosts, files read, or manifest dependencies.
check: For a plugin meant to be suggested, check that its signals match the intended sessions.
quote: When a signal matches and the plugin isn't already installed, Claude Code suggests the plugin in these places:

claim: Relevance signal matching happens locally with no network traffic and no reporting of matched signals to Anthropic or the marketplace operator.
why: Suggestion matching leaves the matched signals and their values on the user’s machine.
check: When reviewing plugin suggestion privacy, check whether the concern is about relevance matching or a different operation such as installation.
quote: Signal matching happens locally on the user's machine and adds no network traffic.

claim: In the terminal, plugin suggestions from a marketplace do not appear until an administrator allowlists it in managed settings via pluginSuggestionMarketplaces, with a source declaration for non-official marketplaces.
why: The source check stops an unrelated source from registering under an allowlisted name.
check: If an org marketplace has relevance blocks but users see no suggestions, check managed settings.
quote: In the terminal, users see no suggestions from a marketplace until an administrator allowlists it in

claim: A plugin `cli` relevance signal uses the leading command Claude runs, after any leading environment assignments and `sudo`.
why: A compound command contributes only its leading command, so `cd infra && terraform plan` records `cd`.
check: Check whether a `cli` signal depends on a command that typically runs second in a compound command.
quote: Claude Code records one command name for each shell command Claude runs: the first token after any leading environment variable assignments and `sudo`.

claim: A recognized `relevance` field over its limit invalidates the entire plugin entry and blocks marketplace installation until corrected.
why: `claude plugin validate` enforces the same field limits.
check: Run `claude plugin validate` on the marketplace and correct any reported relevance limits.
quote: A recognized field whose value exceeds its limit in the [field reference](#field-reference) invalidates the whole plugin entry, and users can't install that plugin from the marketplace until you fix it; `claude plugin validate` reports the same limits.

claim: A plugin suggestion can appear at most once every three sessions across spinner tips and startup notifications, and startup notifications stop after two combined showings.
why: Both types of prompt for the same plugin count toward the startup cutoff.
check: When a startup notification is missing, check the combined count of earlier spinner tips and startup notifications.
quote:
The suggestion appears at most once every three sessions across the spinner tip and the session-start notification combined.
* The session-start notification stops appearing once the spinner tip and the notification have shown the plugin a combined total of two times.

claim: By default, `claude plugin eval` runs each case three times per arm and scores the arm using the mean of its runs.
why: A single run of a non-deterministic agent tells little.
check: Check the configured run count when interpreting the stability of an eval result.
quote: One run of a non-deterministic agent tells you little, so each case runs three times by default. A run's score is the fraction of its graders that passed, weighted if you set weights, and the case's score is the mean across its runs.

claim: By default, plugin evals report `WITH`, `W/OUT`, and their delta, and matching scores of 1.0 show that the case also passed without the plugin.
why: A high score alone does not show the plugin helped.
check: When both arms ran, use the delta to assess what the plugin contributed to the evaluated case.
quote: If a case scores 1.0 both with and without the plugin, the plugin isn't what made it pass.

claim: To test whether Claude chooses a plugin skill, write an eval prompt in natural user language without naming the skill and add a `tool_used: Skill` grader.
why: A failing Skill grader alongside a near-zero delta can show Claude did not choose the skill for that phrasing.
check: Check that trigger prompts do not name or invoke the skill directly and that the grader records its activation.
quote: The most common first finding is a `Δ` near zero with the case's `tool_used: Skill` grader failing, which means Claude isn't choosing your skill on natural phrasing.

claim: In two-arm plugin evals, `tool_used` graders for `Skill` default to invocation indicators unless set to `arm: both` or every grader would be excluded.
why: Counting them would drag the baseline toward zero and inflate delta.
check: Check whether the Skill grader is marked as an indicator before interpreting the case score or delta.
quote:
Claude Code excludes such graders from the score in both arms and reports them in the with-arm as pass/fail indicators only. That includes:

* Every `tool_used` grader whose `tool` is `Skill`

claim: Give each plugin eval case a grader for the result and a grader for the steps Claude took.
why: Together they show whether the answer was right and whether the plugin produced it.
check: Check that cases grade the answer or artifact and separately inspect the relevant tool use or tool order.
quote: Give each case one grader on the result, such as the final message or a produced file, and one on the steps Claude took to produce it,

claim: Plugin eval runs omit personal and project configuration, so package required skills, agents, hooks, or MCP declarations in the plugin under test.
why: Case scaffolding can supply files and git state, and managed policy can still restrict a run.
check: Flag cases relying on user or project settings, `CLAUDE.md`, or personal tools, and check required files are supplied as fixtures.
quote: Ship any skills, agents, hooks, or MCP servers a case depends on in the plugin under test, since a [`scaffold_script`](#add-setup-or-history-with-case-yaml) can supply only files and git state.

claim: In CI, pin both plugin eval models, set a cost ceiling, and use `--trust-plugin` to skip the first-run prompt for a plugin you trust.
why: Pinning makes scores comparable across runs, and the list-price ceiling stops new runs once spent while allowing in-flight runs to finish.
check: Check that CI pins both models, bounds cost, and sets `--threshold` to the required with-plugin score when the default does not fit.
quote: Pass `--trust-plugin` so the job never waits at the [first-run trust prompt](#security), pin both models so scores are comparable over time, keep the report local, and set a cost ceiling as an upper limit:

claim: `claude plugin eval` defaults to a 1.0 threshold for the with-plugin score and exits 1 if any case falls below it.
why: The no-plugin delta is reported without affecting the command’s exit code.
check: Check that CI uses a threshold that matches the required with-plugin case score.
quote: `1.0` | A case passes when its with-arm score is at least this. Any case below it makes the command exit 1

claim: claude plugin eval has no custom-code graders; the types are regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists, llm and baseline.
why: Only the first four are free; llm and baseline call a judge model.
check: Budget for judge calls when suites use llm or baseline graders.
quote: There are no custom-code graders.

claim: The skill-creator plugin eval format (evals/evals.json) and claude plugin eval case files are not interchangeable.
why: The in-session skill-creator loop uses its own `evals/evals.json` format.
check: Do not treat a skill-creator evals.json as a claude plugin eval suite.
quote: The two formats aren't interchangeable.

claim: `claude plugin details` estimates always-on and on-invoke tokens for a loaded plugin’s skills, agents, and commands.
why: Always-on estimates count names, descriptions, and `when_to_use`, while on-invoke estimates cover the bodies.
check: Use the per-component rows to find the largest contributors, and use `/context` in a session to inspect MCP tool cost.
quote: each row splits one skill, agent, or command into its always-on share and its on-invoke cost, which is the body that loads only when that component runs. Use the always-on column to find which component contributes most.

claim: To reduce a plugin’s always-on token estimate, shorten its skill and agent descriptions or split a large plugin so users can install just what they need.
why: A shorter skill description can lose the text Claude matched against a request.
check: After shortening a skill description, use a `tool_used: Skill` grader to recheck triggering.
quote:
Shorten skill and agent descriptions.
* Split a large plugin so users install only the components they need.

claim: Claude Code records plugin usage on each installer’s machine and does not automatically send it to the plugin author.
why: Organization administrators can monitor installs and skill activations with OpenTelemetry or the Enterprise Analytics API.
check: Check whether the maintainer can access organization telemetry or ask users to check their local usage.
quote: Claude Code doesn't report a plugin's usage back to its author.

claim: In `/plugin`, eligible enabled marketplace plugins installed by the user move under `Not used recently` after at least 14 days and 10 sessions without use.
why: A plugin with a theme, output style, monitor, or workflow counts as used without a tracked invocation.
check: Before interpreting a missing label, check whether the plugin is enabled, how it was installed, its components, and whether managed enablement or `strictKnownMarketplaces` applies.
quote: On the **Installed** tab of `/plugin`, an enabled marketplace plugin the user installed moves under a **Not used recently** header after at least 14 days and 10 sessions unused.

claim: Official-marketplace plugins show a Context cost estimate before install, highlighted when the always-on figure is 2,000 tokens or more; plugins in your own marketplace show none.
why: It informs install decisions.
check: When checking pre-install visibility, verify whether the plugin comes from the official marketplace and whether its `Every turn:` estimate meets the highlight threshold.
quote: When the always-on figure is 2,000 tokens or more, the `Every turn:` line appears highlighted.

claim: Claude Code redacts or omits third-party plugin names in OpenTelemetry by default, and `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` exposes real names on supported events.
why: By default, only official-marketplace plugin names are reported verbatim, and `plugin_id_hash` can still distinguish third-party plugins on `plugin_loaded`.
check: If a telemetry event lacks a third-party name, check what that event exposes with and without `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` before interpreting counts.
quote: Every other plugin's name is redacted or omitted by default, including a plugin from your organization's own marketplace.

claim: A backgrounded skill fork has the narrower background-subagent tool set, and `background: false` keeps the fork’s full tool set.
why: A skill fork uses a regular agent type, so the exemption for a subagent that forks the current conversation does not apply.
check: If a skill needs a tool outside its background set, check that it sets `background: false`.
quote: If your skill's steps depend on a tool outside that set, set `background: false` to keep the full tool set.

claim: In a local terminal session, a same-named enterprise, personal, or project skill takes over a built-in command’s name while its aliases still run the built-in command.
why: Claude Code resolves the original command and its aliases separately.
check: Check which name callers use when a skill is intended to replace a built-in command.
quote: In a local terminal session, your skill replaces the built-in command, but not its aliases.

claim: A plugin skill and a same-named enterprise, personal, or project skill both load because the plugin skill uses a `/plugin-name:skill-name` command.
why: The plugin’s command has its own namespace.
check: When the names overlap, check that callers use the qualified name for the plugin skill.
quote: Both load, because plugin skills are namespaced as `/plugin-name:skill-name` |

claim: Use forward slashes in skill file paths, including on Windows.
why: Unix-style paths are portable, while Windows-style paths can fail on Unix.
check: Look for backslash-separated paths in skill instructions and resources.
quote: Always use forward slashes in file paths, even on Windows:

claim: If a skill uses MCP tools, refer to them with fully qualified names such as `ServerName:tool_name`.
why: Qualified references help avoid tool-not-found errors.
check: Check MCP references for the server name and the tool name.
quote: If your Skill uses MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools, always use fully qualified tool names to avoid “tool not found” errors.

claim: Claude Code silently ignores misspelled output-style frontmatter fields.
why: An ignored field does not apply the setting the author intended.
check: Check for misspelled `name`, `description`, `keep-coding-instructions`, and `force-for-plugin` keys.
quote: A misspelled field is ignored without an error.

claim: Claude Code saves user edits to a read-only plugin theme as a copy in the user’s themes directory.
why: A plugin theme appears alongside user themes in `/theme`, so it can be selected and customized there.
check: Check the user’s themes directory for overrides when a customized plugin theme differs from the shipped file.
quote: Plugin themes are read-only, so when a user edits one in `/theme`, the edit is saved as a copy in their own themes directory.

claim: Only a plugin’s `cwd` relevance signal can match at session start, before the first user message.
why: A startup notification depends on a match against the session’s working directory.
check: Check the `cwd` patterns for plugins intended to be suggested at session start.
quote: `cwd` is the only signal that can match at session start, before the user sends a first message.

claim: Use `regex` graders for long plugin eval outputs and reserve `llm` graders for short outputs with concrete PASS and FAIL criteria.
why: A regex can check the whole generated file the same way each time.
check: Look for LLM graders judging long outputs and check whether short-output rubrics define concrete pass and fail conditions.
quote: For long output such as a generated file, grade it with a `regex` grader over the file's contents, which checks the whole file the same way every time. Keep `llm` graders for short outputs, with rubrics written as concrete PASS and FAIL conditions.
